clue.text: With onset of spring, year's going to flourish — date to get involved

definitions.text: With onset of spring, year's going to flourish — date to get involved

indicators.note: the onset of a word is its beginning, so only the opening letter of spring is used
to flourish is to wave about extravagantly, so these letters are waved into a new order
letters that get involved become tangled together, a second signal that the pool is mixed

parts.note: taken as written, apostrophe dropped
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A seasonal saying: as spring begins, the year is set to bloom, and some date is bound up in it.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram, signalled by 'to flourish' and 'to get involved', mixes S with YEARS, GOING and DATE. The whole clue also describes the day: 23 April falls early in spring, England's patron saint's feast.
explanation.definitionFit: England's patron saint's feast falls on 23 April, a date early in spring as the year starts to bloom.

clue.text: Elgar & Co? They're not all English but they may all be barking

definitions.meaning: Elgar is this puzzle's compiler, one of those who make crosswords

definitions.text: They're not all English but they may all be barking
definitions.meaning: dogs: English, Irish and Gordon breeds, all able to bark

explanation.definitionFit: Crossword compilers are called setters, and setters are also gundog breeds, the English one among several.

clue.text: Doctor medicated, peeled lemon infusion?

indicators.note: to doctor is to tamper with, so the letters are altered into a new order
a peeled word loses its outer skin, its first and last letters

explanation.surface: A doctor has medicated someone with a lemon infusion, peeled fruit and all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'peeled' strips M and D from medicated, leaving EDICATE for 'Doctor' to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Iced tea is often served with lemon, a chilled infusion of tea leaves, so the question mark marks an example.

clue.text: Three headers from Fleetwood Town old guard compound this dip in new form

indicators.note: to compound is to mix together, so these letters are combined anew
in new form says the combined letters are recast into a fresh order, backing up the first signal

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the headers of the words are their first letters

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Three headed goals by an old defender at Fleetwood Town, a League football club, transform a slumping side.
explanation.walkthrough: 'compound' mixes THREE, FT and OLD GUARD; 'this ... in new form' just restates that the letters are recast. Fleetwood Town is an English football club. A dip is a pickpocket.
explanation.definitionFit: The Artful Dodger is the young pickpocket in Dickens's Oliver Twist, and dip is slang for a pickpocket.

clue.text: Religious letter about York's top architectural structure

indicators.note: about means around, so the letter goes inside

parts.note: an epistle is a letter, especially one of the apostles' letters in the New Testament

indicators.note: the top of a word in a down clue is its first letter

explanation.surface: A religious letter about the head of York, perhaps the Archbishop, concerns a building.
explanation.definitionFit: An epistyle is the architrave, the beam resting on the column capitals of a classical building.

clue.text: In your full English, one ____ or two? (More ill-advised)

definitions.text: In your full English, one ____ or two?
definitions.meaning: a slice of bacon, served one or two to a full English breakfast

explanation.walkthrough: A full English is the British cooked breakfast of bacon, eggs and sausages.
explanation.definitionFit: A rasher is a bacon slice, and rasher is also the comparative of rash, meaning more reckless.

clue.text: A singer entertains Wimbledon's gate in verses, on occasion flanked by partners who were court specialists

indicators.note: flanked by means with these on either side

parts.note: former partners are exes
a, as in 'a head', means per

indicators.note: entertains means holds inside as a guest

parts.note: the tit is a small songbird

indicators.note: the gate to a word is its first letter, the way in
on occasion means now and then, taking every other letter

explanation.surface: A singer entertains the Wimbledon crowd in verse at times, as Cliff Richard famously did in the rain, flanked by tennis partners.
explanation.walkthrough: Cliff Richard sang to the rain-delayed Wimbledon crowd in 1996, the surface's picture. 'per head' shows why A means PER; 'gate' is the first letter, the way in.
explanation.definitionFit: Expert witnesses give specialist evidence in a law court, so they are specialists in court.

clue.text: Checker with Guardian back catalogues?

indicators.note: back means the run is read in reverse
catalogues is a verb here: the phrase lists, so contains, the letters in a run

explanation.surface: A newspaper's back catalogue of the Guardian checked over.
explanation.walkthrough: The run THGUARD sits in 'with Guardian'; 'back' turns it round.
explanation.definitionFit: A checker is the American name for a draughts piece, the round counter in that board game.

clue.text: 'Queer old Dean' and case of under-secretary's capital

indicators.note: queer means odd, so the letters are made odd by rearranging

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the case of a word is its outer shell, first and last letters

explanation.surface: 'Queer old Dean', Spooner's famous slip for 'dear old Queen', and an under-secretary's case in the capital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Queer' mixes O, DEAN and UY, the outside of under-secretary. Spooner, the Oxford dean, reputedly toasted 'the queer old dean'.
explanation.definitionFit: Yaoundé is the capital city of Cameroon in west-central Africa.

clue.text: Not long after twist, we play out Midsomer Murders

definitions.note: plural 'we' matches the plural answer, the instruments speaking

indicators.note: a small twist here swaps a pair of neighbouring letters in the phrase

parts.note: 'three mins' later is not long after, giving the phrase three mins

explanation.surface: Not long after a plot twist, the theme music of the TV detective drama Midsomer Murders plays out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'twist' swaps the R and the E next to it in THREE MINS. Midsomer Murders is a long-running British TV detective series whose theme tune famously features the theremin.
explanation.definitionFit: The Midsomer Murders theme tune is played on a theremin, an electronic instrument played without touch, so these instruments speak as its players.

clue.text: One often seen with Elton at openings, performing in a Northern orchestra

indicators.note: the openings of the following words are their first letters, read in order

explanation.surface: Elton John, often seen performing in an orchestra from the north of England.
explanation.definitionFit: Elton John is almost always pictured seated at a grand piano, his instrument on stage.

clue.text: No danger here? Empty threat? Distorted picture

indicators.note: distorted letters are bent out of shape into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: an empty word has lost its inside, leaving only its outer letters

explanation.surface: Reassurance that there is no danger, then a dismissive remark about an empty threat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Empty' leaves TT from threat; 'Distorted' mixes those with NO DANGER HERE.
explanation.definitionFit: A picture is an old word for a film, and Enter the Dragon is the 1973 Bruce Lee martial-arts movie.

clue.text: See 11
Bob's Greasy Spoon — time-honoured location for builders

parts.note: a bob was the old British shilling, abbreviated S
a greasy spoon is a cheap café, in British slang a caff
time-honoured means old, long established

explanation.surface: Bob's greasy-spoon café, long the traditional haunt of builders at breakfast.
explanation.walkthrough: A bob is the pre-decimal British shilling, abbreviated S; a caff is British slang for a cheap café.
explanation.definitionFit: Builders work up on scaffolding, the temporary frame of poles and planks around a building site.

clue.text: What shredded parts of Downland areas?

definitions.note: the clue's plural stands for the broad stretch of land the answer names

indicators.note: parts is a verb here: the shuffled letters part SE, splitting it open

parts.note: the South Downs lie in south-east England, abbreviated SE

indicators.note: shredded letters are torn up and rearranged

explanation.surface: A puzzled question about what tore up parts of the Downland areas.
explanation.walkthrough: The South Downs are chalk hills in south-east England. 'parts' is a verb, the mixed letters splitting the abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: A swathe is a broad strip or tract of land, so it stands for extensive areas of countryside.

clue.text: Sustaining the party between Ed and Jezza, perhaps, can I get beaten?

indicators.note: sustaining means holding up, so the can contains the rest

parts.note: a can is a tin

indicators.note: between leaders Ed Miliband and Jeremy Corbyn the party briefly had no leader, so loses its first letter

parts.note: the party here is Labour, the UK party

explanation.surface: Supporting Labour in its interregnum between Ed Miliband and Jeremy Corbyn, can I take a beating?
explanation.walkthrough: Labour was leaderless between Ed Miliband's resignation and Jeremy 'Jezza' Corbyn's election in 2015, so LABOUR loses its leader L.
explanation.definitionFit: A tabourin is a small drum, an instrument that is beaten with sticks.

clue.text: With spirits low, CAMRA finally quits Olympia, sadly

indicators.note: sadly works as a signal that the remaining letters are rearranged
quits means leaves, so that letter is taken out of the venue's name
finally points to the last letter of the campaign's name

explanation.surface: The Campaign for Real Ale finally leaves Olympia, the London venue of its beer festival, to everyone's regret.
explanation.walkthrough: CAMRA is the Campaign for Real Ale; 'quits' takes its last letter A out of OLYMPIA, and 'sadly' mixes OLYMPI.
explanation.definitionFit: Moping is being dejected, so to act mopily is to act in low spirits.

clue.text: Possibly murderous Colonel curses full lifts — what's with his beef?

indicators.note: lifts in a down clue raises the letters, reading them upwards

parts.note: curses! and drat! are both mild oaths
the full amount is the sum

explanation.surface: A possibly murderous colonel swears at full lifts; what's he got against his beef?
explanation.walkthrough: Colonel Mustard is a suspect in the board game Cluedo; mustard is also the classic condiment with roast beef.
explanation.definitionFit: Colonel Mustard is a Cluedo suspect, and mustard is the hot condiment eaten alongside roast beef.

clue.text: Where Lewis goes to change line-up? It's to plain clothes

indicators.note: clothes is a verb here: the words clothe, so contain, the answer

explanation.surface: Where Lewis goes to change his line-up? It's to plain clothes.
explanation.walkthrough: Lewis is Lewis Hamilton, the Formula One driver, who changes tyres in the pits; 'Lewis' and 'change' suggest the TV detective Inspector Lewis.
explanation.definitionFit: A pit stop is where a racing driver halts for tyre changes and refuelling mid-race.

clue.text: Some Spoonerish back-slappery? John Bull may wear it today

definitions.text: John Bull may wear it today

indicators.note: Spoonerish means the opening sounds of the two words are swapped

parts.note: some, as in 'some party!', is a hearty or enthusiastic qualifier, read here as hearty
back-slappery is a pat on the back

explanation.surface: Some jovial back-slapping on the day the figure of John Bull, England personified, dresses up for a party.
explanation.walkthrough: John Bull is the cartoon personification of England; 'today' is St George's Day, the puzzle's theme.
explanation.definitionFit: A paper party hat is festive headgear that an English patriot might don at a celebration of the national day.

clue.text: An Englishman abroad, maybe spending year in holidaying wildly

indicators.note: wildly means the leftover letters are arranged anyhow
spending means using up, so those letters are lost

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An Englishman abroad, perhaps away for a year, holidaying wildly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'spending' takes Y and IN out of holidaying, leaving HOLIDAG for 'wildly' to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: A hidalgo is a Spanish gentleman, so 'Englishman abroad' is the cryptic way of putting a foreign counterpart of an English gent.

clue.text: What's said to comfort my mum, taking a dip here in Aquae Sulis?

indicators.note: taking a dip means going into the water, so ma goes inside

parts.note: 'there, there' is what is said to comfort someone
ma is mum, mother

explanation.surface: Something said to comfort my mum as she takes a dip in the Roman baths at Bath.
explanation.walkthrough: Aquae Sulis was the Roman name for Bath, the English city famous for its Roman baths.
explanation.definitionFit: Thermae were the public baths of ancient Rome, such as those at Aquae Sulis, modern Bath.

clue.text: Her Majesty's right — yes! — to party with these mods

indicators.note: to party is to whoop it up, so the letters are thrown about

parts.note: the words of Her Majesty, the apostrophe s dropped
taken as written

explanation.surface: The Queen is correct to say yes to a party with these mods.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to party' shows the letters of HER MAJESTY are a mix of R, YES and the answer. The Jam were a 1970s-80s British mod revival band led by Paul Weller.
explanation.definitionFit: The Jam were a British band of the mod revival, styled in sharp suits like 1960s mods.

clue.text: Not even James Bond backs engaging criminal to hunt for burial site

indicators.note: engaging means taking in, holding the shuffled letters inside
backs means the remaining letters are read backwards
not even means without the word even, so those letters go

parts.note: Bond is agent double-oh-seven, written OO SEVEN
taken as written

indicators.note: criminal suggests the letters are bent into a new order

explanation.surface: Not even James Bond supports involving a criminal in a manhunt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not even' removes the word even from Bond's number, leaving OOS; 'backs' gives SOO; 'criminal' mixes TO HUNT into UTTONH, which 'engaging' puts inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Sutton Hoo in Suffolk is the Anglo-Saxon ship burial ground where a king's grave goods were found.

clue.text: Picnickers in woods surprisingly clipped our Eagle?

indicators.note: clipped means trimmed at both ends, losing first and last letters

parts.note: the song Teddy Bears' Picnic promises a big surprise down in the woods, where the teddies picnic

explanation.surface: Picnickers in the woods unexpectedly trimmed something belonging to our eagle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'If you go down to the woods today, you're sure of a big surprise' opens the song Teddy Bears' Picnic. Eddie 'the Eagle' Edwards was Britain's endearingly hopeless 1988 Olympic ski jumper.
explanation.definitionFit: Eddie the Eagle was the nickname of Britain's famous amateur Olympic ski jumper, a national favourite.

clue.text: Mixing a G'n'T, I like Tim Peake's habit when coming down!

definitions.text: like Tim Peake's habit when coming down!

indicators.note: mixing a drink stirs it up, so these letters are stirred into a new order

parts.note: gin and tonic written as its letters G, N and T

explanation.surface: Mixing a gin and tonic, I am like the astronaut Tim Peake with his habit when returning to Earth.
explanation.walkthrough: Tim Peake is a British astronaut; his 'habit' is his suit, the anti-g suit worn to resist gravity's force on re-entry.
explanation.definitionFit: An anti-g suit counters gravitational pressure on the body, which astronauts wear during descent.

clue.text: Anthem ahead of Lord's Test? Passing round fine beer, newly heartening jingoism

indicators.note: newly heartening gives the word a new heart, its middle letters replaced
passing round turns the word for fine back the other way

parts.note: fine, as in 'OK', means sure
ale is a beer

explanation.surface: A patriotic anthem before a cricket Test at Lord's, with fine beer passed round, inspiring fresh jingoism.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Passing round' gives ERUS, which with the beer replaces INGOIS, the heart of jingoism. Lord's is London's famous cricket ground, where Jerusalem is sung before England matches.
explanation.definitionFit: Blake's hymn Jerusalem serves as England's unofficial national anthem, sung at cricket Tests at Lord's.

clue.text: Harrods to take one hard look following conduct in vocal exchange

indicators.note: vocal also means of vowels, so two vowels exchange places
following sends the hard look second, after the word for conduct

parts.note: conduct means behaviour, deportment
a stare is a hard look

explanation.surface: Harrods, the grand London shop, has a hard look at someone's behaviour during a heated spoken exchange.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in vocal exchange' swaps the O of the first word with the A of the second, giving DEPARTMENT STORE; vocal can mean 'of vowels'. 'to take one' is linking padding.
explanation.definitionFit: Harrods in Knightsbridge is London's most famous big shop selling everything in separate sections.
